questions.bok: Sources and uses of reliability data
questions.stem:
Five units are on a fixed-time test. Failed units are not replaced. Suspended units count only to the censoring time. The point estimate uses total unit time and the failure count.
\[
\hat\theta=\frac{T}{r}
\]
What is the estimated mean life?
questions.why: Add the failure times and the time on every suspended unit. Then divide by the number of failures. \[ T=30+70+3(80)=340 \] \[ \hat\theta=340/2=170 \] 50 hours averages only the two failure times. 80 hours is the censoring time. 340 hours is the total time before dividing by the failures. C. 170 hours

traps.A: Averages the failure times and drops the suspensions.
traps.D: Stops at the total unit time.

chart.title: Censored life test
chart.altText: Two units failed at 30 hours and 70 hours. The other three were still operating when the test stopped at 80 hours.

questions.stem:
A sampling plan accepts a lot only when a sample of 5 contains no defectives. The lot fraction defective is 0.20, and units are independent.
\[
P_a=(1-p)^{n}
\]
What is the probability of acceptance, to four decimal places?
questions.why: Acceptance requires five good units. \[ P_a=(0.80)^{5}=0.3277 \] 0.2000 is the lot fraction defective. 0.6723 is the probability of finding at least one defective. 0.8000 is the probability that one unit is good. B. 0.3277

traps.C: Reports the probability that the lot is rejected.

chart.title: Zero-defect sampling plan
chart.altText: The sample size is 5. The lot is accepted only when the sample has zero defectives. The lot fraction defective is 0.20.

questions.stem:
Process performance \(P_p\) uses the specification width and the process standard deviation. It does not use the process mean.
\[
P_p=\frac{USL-LSL}{6\sigma}
\]
What is \(P_p\)?
questions.why: Use the full specification width in the numerator and six standard deviations in the denominator. \[ P_p=\frac{130-70}{6(5)}=2.00 \] 1.33 is \(C_{pk}\), which uses the nearer specification and three standard deviations. 4.00 uses three standard deviations in the \(P_p\) denominator. 12.0 divides the width by one standard deviation. B. 2.00

traps.A: Computes the one-sided capability from the off-center mean.

chart.title: Specification and process spread
chart.altText: The lower specification is 70, the upper specification is 130, the process mean is 90, and the process standard deviation is 5.

questions.stem:
Three identical units are independent. The function works if at least two units work. Each unit has mission reliability \(R\).
\[
R_{2/3}=3R^{2}(1-R)+R^{3}
\]
What is the mission reliability of the function?
questions.why: At least two includes exactly two and all three. \[ 3(0.80)^{2}(0.20)=0.384 \] \[ (0.80)^{3}=0.512 \] \[ R_{2/3}=0.384+0.512=0.896 \] 0.384 is exactly two survivors. 0.512 is all three. 0.800 is one unit. D. 0.896

traps.C: Uses the reliability of one unit.

chart.title: Two-out-of-three function
chart.altText: Three identical independent units each have mission reliability 0.80. At least two must work.

questions.stem: The team does not rank these two open modes by the product of the ratings. Its stated rule is that severity 9 or 10 is High action priority even when that product is smaller. Which mode is first under that rule?
options: Mode A. Severity 9 is High under the stated rule.
Mode B. Its product, 120, is larger.
Mode B. Occurrence 6 is the largest single rating in the table.
Neither. Both detection ratings are below 6.
questions.why: The stated rule puts severity 9 ahead of a larger product. \[ RPN_A=9\times 2\times 2=36 \] \[ RPN_B=5\times 6\times 4=120 \] Mode B would be first if the team ranked by the product. It does not. Detection below 6 is not the stated rule. A. Mode A. Severity 9 is High under the stated rule.

traps.B: Ranks by the product after the stem says not to.
traps.C: Ranks by the largest single rating.

chart.title: Action-priority comparison
chart.altText: Mode A has severity 9, occurrence 2, and detection 2. Mode B has severity 5, occurrence 6, and detection 4. Severity 9 or 10 is High action priority.

questions.stem:
Fault density is the number of discovered faults divided by the size of the code, in thousands of lines.
\[
D=\frac{N}{K}
\]
What is the fault density?
questions.why: Divide the fault count by the code size. Do not invert the ratio. \[ D=12/24=0.5 \] 2 inverts the ratio. 12 is the fault count. 24 is the code size. A. 0.5 per thousand lines

traps.B: Divides the code size by the fault count.

chart.title: Discovered software faults
chart.altText: The test found 12 faults in 24 thousand lines of code.

questions.stem:
One unit has a constant mean time between failures. It operates \(H\) hours per year.
\[
f=\frac{H}{\theta}
\]
How many failures are expected per year?
questions.why: Divide the annual operating hours by the mean time between failures. \[ f=4000/50000=0.08 \] 0.02 would be correct for 1,000 operating hours. 12.5 inverts the ratio. 50,000 hours is the mean time between failures. B. 0.08

traps.C: Divides the mean life by the annual hours.

chart.title: Annual exposure
chart.altText: The mean time between failures is 50,000 hours. The unit operates 4,000 hours per year.

questions.stem:
The required factor of safety is \(n\). The calculated stress is \(\sigma\). The material allowable must satisfy
\[
S_{req}=n\sigma
\]
What allowable strength is required?
questions.why: Multiply the calculated stress by the required factor. Do not divide. \[ S_{req}=2(150)=300 \] 75 MPa divides the stress by the factor. 150 MPa is the calculated stress. 2 is the factor, not a strength. C. 300 MPa

traps.A: Divides the stress by the factor.

chart.title: Required strength
chart.altText: The calculated stress is 150 MPa. The required factor of safety is 2.

questions.stem:
A two-level fractional factorial uses \(k\) factors and \(p\) generators.
\[
N=2^{k-p}
\]
How many runs are in this half fraction?
questions.why: A half fraction of four two-level factors uses one generator. \[ k-p=4-1=3 \] \[ N=2^{3}=8 \] 4 is the number of factors. 15 is one less than the full factorial. 16 is the full \(2^{4}\) design. B. 8

traps.C: Subtracts one from the full factorial.

chart.title: Half fraction of four factors
chart.altText: There are 4 two-level factors. The design is a half fraction, so p is 1.

questions.stem:
A repairable unit must meet availability \(A\). Its mean time between failures is fixed. The longest mean repair time that still meets the availability is
\[
MTTR=\frac{MTBF(1-A)}{A}
\]
What is that maximum mean repair time?
questions.why: Put the unavailability in the numerator and divide by the availability. \[ MTBF(1-A)=190(0.05)=9.5 \] \[ MTTR=9.5/0.95=10 \] 9.5 hours stops before dividing by \(A\). 180 hours subtracts that 10-hour repair limit from the 190-hour mean life. 200 hours adds the 10-hour repair to the 190-hour mean life. A. 10 hours

traps.C: Subtracts the repair limit from the MTBF.
traps.D: Adds the allowable repair time to the MTBF and reports the sum.

chart.title: Availability requirement
chart.altText: The required availability is 0.95. The mean time between failures is 190 hours.
